title: The Judges Who Walk Between Gardens
summary: A physician’s civic reforms and traveling musicians support self-governing settlements divided by occupation and competing charters.
source_notes: A physician-reformer confronting military and religious privileges becomes an attempt to unite practical civic jurisdiction.
Exiled musicians blending traditions and carrying political memory become a traveling valley ensemble using pre-industrial instruments.
Partition, occupation, a independence vote, and destructive withdrawal become the eastern gardens’ interrupted self-government.
Rural communal autonomy and elected adjudicators become walking judges without a hereditary sovereign.

entries.title: Valen the Basin Physician
entries.body:
Valen treated soldiers and gardeners through the same queue, then proposed ending their separate courts. His former ally called the reform dangerous. Surviving patient accounts show ordinary cooperation persisting after the political alliance collapsed.

Later accounts make Valen the Basin Physician the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Judges Who Walk Between Gardens. Suth’s garden communes elected judges rather than inheriting a sovereign. In 943 a physician reformer sought to reduce the separate courts maintained by armed households and funerary custodians. His ally withdrew support when those institutions threatened revolt. Traveling musicians carried arguments between valleys, blending older measures with instruments learned in exile. An outside authority later occupied the eastern gardens while the western communes retained a different charter. When a public vote ended occupation, departing forces destroyed channels and records. Returning households therefore faced reconstruction before constitutional celebration. The elected judges now walk between settlements to hear claims, because neither the old exemptions nor the new vote can make water flow through a broken canal.

In the connected record, [The Eastern Broken Gardens](b020-the-eastern-broken-gardens.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Coerced Transfer Review](b020-the-coerced-transfer-review.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: how elected courts can rebuild channels while deciding which occupation-era transactions were coerced and which present households depend upon them.
entries.background: The Suth valleys cultivate grafted orchards and irrigated gardens amid dry hills. Food production depends on precise local knowledge: when to open a channel, which rootstock tolerates mineral water, and how many hands a harvest requires. Asylum customs let strangers work under temporary names, but temporary recognition does not automatically convey inheritance. The same gardens can preserve an old promise and expose its injustice. A court that assigns water without accounting for the labor of keeping it clean may issue a valid judgment that no household can afford to obey.

entries.title: The Eastern Broken Gardens
entries.body:
Returning households found gates burned and channels blocked. Constitutional visitors planted ceremonial trees before supplying tools. Gardeners recorded both gifts, demonstrating that symbolic return and practical recovery were different achievements.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Walking Judges
entries.body:
Judges visit gardens rather than requiring every claimant to travel. Their elections exclude servants in several communes. Reformers propose widening the electorate while preserving the accessible hearings that already provide a genuine alternative to inherited office.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Ally’s Reversal
entries.body:
Valen’s ally withdrew support after privileged courts threatened supply boycotts. Later songs describe personal treachery alone. Grain accounts reveal the threat’s force, explaining the choice without removing responsibility for abandoning promised reforms.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Exile’s Reed Lute
entries.body:
The lute combines a local body with a tuning learned abroad. Cultural custodians call the arrangement impure. Musicians show how changed materials allowed continuity in exile, refusing an account of heritage that would prohibit the adaptations sustaining it.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Judge’s Shared Meal
entries.body:
Claimants eat together before a hearing if they consent. Refusal does not count against a case. The limit prevents hospitality from becoming forced reconciliation, particularly where people harmed during occupation face neighbors who benefited from their absence.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Charter of No Inherited Seat
entries.body:
The charter forbids hereditary judges but leaves eligibility tied to landholding. Families maintain influence through property. Readers distinguish the real achievement of elected office from the claim that election alone eliminated inherited power.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Channel Root Eel
entries.body:
Small eels travel through root-lined irrigation channels and disappear when gates remain closed too long. Gardeners use their return to assess reconnection. Celebrants call them liberated ancestors, overlooking the living habitat that reconstruction has restored.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Judges’ Graft Road
entries.body:
The road follows settlements needing seasonal graft inspections, allowing hearings and practical instruction on one journey. Wealthier communes seek priority visits. Judges publish travel costs and unmet requests so exclusion cannot disappear behind their title of universal service.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Coerced Transfer Review
entries.body:
Occupation-era deeds require inquiry into actual consent and subsequent dependency. The rule does not void every transfer automatically. It creates space for restitution that recognizes both original harm and households now relying on a garden they acquired under different circumstances.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Vote and the Gate Fires
entries.body:
The vote ended outside rule but departing forces burned gatehouses and channel controls. Later ceremonies merge decision and liberation into one moment. Reconstruction records show years of labor required before many households experienced the freedom publicly announced.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Physician’s Two Queue Tiles
entries.body:
One tile once marked soldiers and the other gardeners. Valen turned both downward beneath a shared bench. Curators want them displayed upright, while patients prefer the bench’s continued use as evidence that the institutional distinction was practically challenged.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Song’s Visiting Verse
entries.body:
Each host garden adds a verse naming its current repair need. Distant audiences prefer a fixed performance. Musicians retain the changing verse, keeping the ensemble connected to practical communities rather than becoming a portable image of rebellion.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The First Return Inventories
entries.body:
Inventories distinguish destruction, neglect, and supplies taken by neighbors. Their precision prevents every loss being assigned to one dramatic withdrawal. It also names local beneficiaries whose role later patriotic accounts preferred to omit.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Judge’s Empty Footsteps
entries.body:
Footsteps recur on an abandoned hearing path after a claimant dies unanswered. Rain channels explain some sounds but not their timing. Judges have begun recording postponed cases publicly, responding to an actual unfinished duty without claiming certainty about the phenomenon.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Graft Recovery Teaching
entries.body:
Teachers demonstrate grafts using local rootstocks and bounded water. Reconstruction donors supply prestigious imported varieties poorly suited to damaged channels. Gardeners request useful materials instead, turning gratitude into a negotiation over what assistance can actually accomplish.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Servants’ Election Petition
entries.body:
Servants maintain communal channels but cannot elect the judges ruling upon their work. Their petition invokes contribution rather than a fictitious ancient charter. Commune leaders must decide whether self-government includes those whose labor makes the governing households viable.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
